warmup.q: A payment and its refunds obey one rule: the refunds never add up to more than the payment. Where can a single write check that rule and add a refund, with nothing wrapped around it?
options: Only in a SQL database, inside a transaction (a group of writes that happen together or not at all)
In one MongoDB document that holds the refunds, or in one PostgreSQL row whose JSON column holds them: one guarded update of one record
Only in MongoDB, because PostgreSQL can't change part of a JSON value
Nowhere: a rule over several refunds always needs a transaction across several records
warmup.why: Both databases make a write to one record atomic: it happens completely or not at all, and no other write slips in halfway. Put the refunds inside the record, and the rule is about one record. A single update can then check it in its filter and make the change in the same step. PostgreSQL changes part of a JSON value with jsonb_set, as the fourth section shows. Keep the refunds in records of their own, and the rule spans several records. Then it does need a transaction.

sections.h: A document holds one payment and everything read with it
sections.html:
In a SQL database such as PostgreSQL, a payment with two refunds is three rows in two tables. The payment screen joins them back together, combining the rows that share a payment id. MongoDB stores a document instead. A document is one record shaped like JSON, the text format that writes data as names and values inside curly braces, with lists in square brackets. Here's the payment from the Try-it below, after its first refund:

{ _id: "pay-81002", status: "SETTLED", amountMinor: 6837,      // other fields left out
  refundedMinor: 6000,
  refunds: [ { refundId: "ref-1", amountMinor: 6000 } ] }

MongoDB calls a set of documents a collection, the way SQL has tables. Every document has an _id, its primary key, unique in its collection. On disk and over the network, a document travels as BSON, binary JSON. BSON adds the types JSON lacks: 32- and 64-bit whole numbers, Decimal128 for exact decimals, a date, ObjectId (a generated id) and raw bytes. A document can be at most 16 MB.

Let's build the payment one version at a time. Version 1 copies the tables: a payments collection and a refunds collection, each refund holding its payment's id. That's called referencing. The screen now makes two reads. Worse, the rule "refunds never add up to more than the payment" spans two documents. Checking and writing it safely then needs a multi-document transaction: a group of writes to several documents that happen together or not at all.

Version 2 puts the refunds inside the payment, in an array, next to a running total, refundedMinor. That's called embedding. One read returns everything the screen shows. And in MongoDB, a write to one document is atomic: it happens completely or not at all, and no other write can slip in halfway. So one updateOne, the command that changes one document, can check the rule and change it. Its filter says "only if refundedMinor plus this refund is at most amountMinor". Its update adds the refund to the array and the amount to the total. Two refunds that race for the last 60.00 can't both win, because the second one's filter no longer matches. That's the bakery from the opening, solved with one write.

So what should live inside? Model the access patterns first gave MongoDB's own rule. Embed what's read together, changed together and stays small: a payment has a handful of refunds at most. Reference what grows without limit, like an account's payments over the years.

Types matter more than they look. mongosh, MongoDB's shell (the program where you type commands), stores a small whole number as a 32-bit int. A Kotlin Long sent through the Java driver, the library a Kotlin or Java program uses to talk to MongoDB, becomes a 64-bit long. Say an old import job, a program that once copied payments in from another system, sent an amount as the text "42.50". It's stored as text, and every sum skips it.

That's where "NoSQL means no schema" goes wrong. A schema is the set of rules for what a record must hold. A collection has no fixed columns, but you can attach a validator, a $jsonSchema rule that every write must pass. A write that breaks it is refused with error 121, "Document failed validation", and told which rule failed. The default level, strict, checks every insert and update, but not the documents already there. MongoDB 9.0 added a stricter level, constraint. To switch it on, MongoDB scans the whole collection and refuses if any document breaks the rules; from then on, every document passes. MongoDB 9.0 also checks every incoming BSON document by default, so a damaged one is refused at the door. The Try-it trips over the old text amount.

In MongoDB, the document is the unit of everything. Keep what must change together inside one document. The rest of this lesson follows the document into an index, through a pipeline, into PostgreSQL and across three servers. First, the index.

aside.title: Doesn't MongoDB have transactions?
aside.html: It does. Since version 4.0, MongoDB can group writes to several documents into one transaction, all or nothing, the way DynamoDB single-table design and transactions did. MongoDB's own docs say such a transaction usually costs more than a write to one document, and that embedding stays the better design in most cases. So keep transactions for data that really can't share a document, such as a transfer between two accounts. The Transactions track's lesson on transactions in NoSQL reads their fine print.

sections.h: An index is a sorted list of keys, and explain() shows what it did
sections.html:
The shop dashboard asks for shop M-0042's newest FAILED payments. Model the access patterns first called that question AP3, the third of the six questions this app asks, and built an index for it: { merchantId: 1, status: 1, createdAt: -1 }. Its cost() helper summed up MongoDB's explain() report in four numbers. Let's see where each number comes from, because reading these reports is how you check any query.

An index works like the catalogue in a library: a sorted list of keys, each pointing at one document, so nobody has to walk every shelf. This one is sorted by shop, then status, then time, newest first (that's the -1). explain() describes the plan MongoDB ran as a chain of stages. IXSCAN walks a range of the index, and keysExamined counts the keys it touched. FETCH loads the document behind each key, and docsExamined counts those. COLLSCAN reads every document in the collection. SORT sorts in memory, because no index gives the order the query wants.

In a healthy query, keys examined, documents examined and documents returned are close together, like that lesson's 5, 5 and 5. When thousands of keys or documents are read to return five, the index doesn't match the query.

A query can skip the documents altogether. If it asks only for fields the index holds, and leaves out _id, MongoDB answers from the index alone. That's a covered query: the plan says PROJECTION_COVERED, and docsExamined is 0. A screen that lists only times and amounts can be served that way.

Arrays get one index entry per element. An index on refunds.refundId is a multikey index: a payment with three refunds has three entries, each pointing at the same payment. "Which payment does refund ref-1 belong to?" becomes a lookup of one key. Every write pays for every entry, though, so a payment with 20 refunds updates 20 entries in that index.

AP4 needs a unique index, one that refuses a second document with the same key. It's for the idempotency key, a value the app makes once per payment and sends again on every retry, so a retry can't create a second payment. The index hides a trap. A document without the field is indexed as if the field were null, an empty value, and a unique index allows only one null. On a collection where most payments have no key, the index can't even be built. Make it partial, indexing only the documents where the field is text. Then a second use of a key fails with error E11000, "duplicate key".

Each index is one more sorted list that every insert and update must keep up to date. So add one for a question you've written down, and check with explain() that the query uses it. Indexes find documents. To add them up, MongoDB has a different tool, next.

sections.h: Adding up a shop's day: the aggregation pipeline
sections.html:
The finance team wants shop M-0042's day: how many payments per status, the total amount and the largest one. In SQL that's a GROUP BY, which sorts rows into groups by a value and works out a count or a sum for each group. MongoDB's answer is the aggregation pipeline. It's a list of stages, and each stage takes documents in and passes documents on, in order. Picture a line of people at a counter, each doing one job before handing the tray along.

The stages map onto SQL closely enough to translate by hand. $match keeps only the documents that match, like WHERE. $group is GROUP BY: its _id is the grouping key, and accumulators such as $sum, $avg and $max work out the totals. $sort is ORDER BY, $project picks the fields to keep, and $limit stops after a number of documents. $unwind turns one document with an array into one document per element, which is how you'd total refunds across payments. $lookup joins in documents from another collection.

Order matters, because each stage sees only what the stage before it passed on. Put $match first, and the query planner, the part of MongoDB that decides how to run a query, can use an index for it. Then only the matching documents enter the pipeline. The Try-it's plan shows it: GROUP > FETCH > IXSCAN, 202 keys and 200 documents for M-0042's 200 payments. The AP3 index serves the match on merchantId, then has to step over the status part of each key, which it doesn't care about here. That costs the two extra keys. In MongoDB 9.0, the newer engine that runs queries does the $group inside that same plan.

$group and $sort are blocking: they must see every document coming in before they can pass anything on, so they hold it all in memory. Each stage may use 100 MB of memory before it has to spill the rest to disk. MongoDB 9.0 adds a limit for a whole operation: 1 GB or 20% of the server's memory, whichever is bigger. So a report over a year of payments should $match the smallest slice it can, as early as it can.

What about $lookup? It's fine for a report that runs now and then. If the app joins on every read of a busy screen, the document has the wrong shape. Embed the data, or copy the few fields the read needs, the way Model the access patterns first copied a summary of recent payments into the account.

None of this needs MongoDB, though. A SQL database can store a document too, and the next section puts the same payment in PostgreSQL.

sections.h: The same document in PostgreSQL: a jsonb column
sections.html:
Let's store the bakery's payment in PostgreSQL instead. The SQL track's lesson on JSONB showed the tool: a jsonb column holds a JSON value in a binary form that PostgreSQL can search inside. That's the document model inside a relational database, a database of tables. Putting it next to MongoDB shows what the model buys and what the product adds.

Store the payment as one row of payment_doc(id text PRIMARY KEY, doc jsonb NOT NULL), with the refunds inside doc. The refund is still one statement on one record:

UPDATE payment_doc
   SET doc = jsonb_set(
               jsonb_set(doc, '{refundedMinor}', to_jsonb((doc->>'refundedMinor')::bigint + 6000)),
               '{refunds}', doc->'refunds' || '{"refundId": "ref-1", "amountMinor": 6000}')
 WHERE id = 'pay-81002'
   AND doc->>'status' = 'SETTLED'
   AND (doc->>'refundedMinor')::bigint + 6000 <= (doc->>'amountMinor')::bigint;

jsonb_set replaces one value inside the document, and || adds the new refund to the end of the array. One UPDATE is atomic for its row. When two refunds race, the second waits for the first one's row lock, a hold that a statement keeps on a row while it changes it. Then PostgreSQL checks the second one's WHERE again, against the new version of the row. So two refunds of the last 60.00 can't both pass: the same promise as MongoDB's guarded updateOne.

Validation maps too. A CHECK constraint is a rule every row must pass, and it works for the parts of the document you name: CHECK (jsonb_typeof(doc->'amountMinor') = 'number'). ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT scans the table and refuses if any row breaks the rule, which is what MongoDB 9.0's constraint level does. Add NOT VALID, and it checks only new writes, like strict, until VALIDATE CONSTRAINT checks the old rows later.

The differences are in what surrounds the document. PostgreSQL has real joins, a planner that weighs the cost of each way to run a query, and transactions over any rows. So the document can sit next to the ledger and the table of shops. Its GIN index answers containment, "which documents hold this key with this value" (@>), for any key, but not ranges or order. So the fields you sort by usually stay in ordinary columns next to doc. MongoDB indexes paths inside the document in sorted order and caps a document at 16 MB. It also shards a collection on its own: it splits the documents across many machines, which one PostgreSQL server doesn't do. Both rewrite the whole stored document when you change one field, so both want small documents.

I'd decide it this way. If the documents live beside relational data, a jsonb column in the database you already run is usually the better choice. Choose MongoDB when the documents are the system: the main records, read and written whole, at a size or a write rate that will need sharding.

Either way, the document is safe on one machine. The last section asks what happens when that machine stops.

sections.h: When the main server fails: replica sets and which writes survive
sections.html:
So far, MongoDB ran as one mongod, the MongoDB server program, on one machine. When that machine dies, payments stop. So in real use MongoDB runs as a replica set: usually three servers, called members, each holding a copy of the data. One member, the primary, takes every write. It applies the write and records it in its oplog (local.oplog.rs), a list of changes in the order the primary made them. The other members, the secondaries, copy the oplog and replay it. This is leader-based replication: one copy decides the order, and the others follow. Cassandra, in the last lesson, does the opposite: every replica takes writes, and timestamps decide.

Picture a bank branch with a head teller and two assistants. Every change goes to the head teller, who writes it in the day book, in order. The assistants copy the day book, line by line. The head teller is the primary, the day book is the oplog, and the assistants are the secondaries.

If the secondaries hear nothing from the primary for electionTimeoutMillis, 10 seconds by default, one of them calls an election. To become primary, it needs the votes of a majority of members, 2 of 3. The two sides of a broken network can't both hold a majority, so there's never a second primary taking writes for long.

When may the app, the database's client, hear "OK" for a write? That's the write concern. w: 1 answers once the primary has the write. w: "majority", the default since MongoDB 5.0, waits until a majority of members have it. The difference shows only in a failover, when a new primary takes over, and the stepper walks through one. A member votes only for a candidate whose oplog is at least as recent as its own. So a write that a majority holds is sure to be on the new primary. A write that only the old primary had is rolled back when that member rejoins. It's undone and saved to files under <dbpath>/rollback/, in the server's data folder, and the client that got its OK is never told.

That's why lowering the write concern to w: 1 "for speed" is a trap. In a healthy set nothing looks wrong, and the gain is real but small, a few milliseconds. Then a primary is cut off for a few seconds, takes writes no one else sees, and rolls them back later. In the bank, the lines that only the head teller wrote get torn out of the day book and filed in an envelope. The picture breaks on the envelope: in MongoDB, nobody reads it unless someone goes looking.

A write that a majority has survives a failover. Leave payments at w: "majority". And when a write fails with a wtimeout error, treat it as "unknown", not "failed", because the write isn't undone.

The Replication track builds leader-based replication from scratch in its first lesson. The Partitioning track's lesson on running MongoDB covers setting up a replica set, sharding, and the balancer that moves data between shards.

stepper.title: A primary fails over: what w:1 and w:"majority" survive
stepper.intro: Three members, one oplog each. This is the run from the Try-it below, one frame per step.

On the other side, mongo1 can see only itself, a minority, so it steps down. Two sides of a cut can't both hold a majority, so they can't both elect a primary.

try.title: Lose an acknowledged write in a failover
steps: Make sure env/mongo.yml is down. From the labs folder, start a three-member replica set (about 30 seconds, and about 1.5 GB of Docker's memory). env/mongo-rs.yml starts the members, sets up the replica set rs0 and reports healthy once mongo1 is primary.

Run the commands below in order. docker network disconnect cuts mongo1 off from the others, and step 2 has to run within about 10 seconds of it, before mongo1 notices it's alone. Predict which of the four payments are left at the end.
The last command stops the set and deletes its data.

refs.title: MongoDB: rollbacks during replica set failover
MongoDB: write concern (w, wtimeout, the majority default)

opening:
At a bakery, a customer paid 68.37 for a party order, then brought most of it back. Two staff members, at two tills, each press "refund 60.00" in the same second. The rule is that refunds never add up to more than the payment, so only one should go through.

It's easy to think that a rule like that needs a lock around everything: lock the payment, check every refund, write, unlock. It does, if the refunds live in separate records. The way out is to make it a rule about one record.

Wide-column stores with Cassandra kept a payment's history as rows of flat columns. MongoDB, a free database program, stores each record as a document, a tree of fields. In this lesson, we'll put a payment and its refunds in one document and refund it safely with one write. We'll look inside its indexes, add up a shop's day, store the same document in PostgreSQL, and make a server fail on purpose to see which writes survive. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with two refunds of 60.00 racing for one payment of 68.37 at a bakery. With the refunds inside the payment's document, one guarded update checks the rule and writes in the same step, and the second refund finds nothing to change.

Next time an app tells you "saved", ask two questions: saved where, and on how many machines? A save that only one server has heard of can still disappear.

Next, we'll leave nested documents for data that points at itself, like customers who invite other customers, and ask how SQL can follow a chain of any length.

compare.title: A merchant's daily totals: SQL and the aggregation pipeline

a.label: SQL (PostgreSQL)
a.title: SQL (PostgreSQL)
a.html: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS payments, SUM(amount_minor) AS amount_minor, MAX(amount_minor) AS largest FROM payment WHERE merchant_id = 'M-0042' AND created_at >= TIMESTAMP '2026-11-07 00:00:00' AND created_at < TIMESTAMP '2026-11-08 00:00:00' GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

b.label: MongoDB aggregation
b.title: MongoDB aggregation
b.html: db.payments.aggregate([ { $match: { merchantId: "M-0042", // WHERE createdAt: { $gte: ISODate("2026-11-07T00:00:00Z"), $lt: ISODate("2026-11-08T00:00:00Z") } } }, { $group: { _id: "$status", // GROUP BY payments: { $sum: 1 }, // COUNT(*) amountMinor: { $sum: "$amountMinor" }, // SUM largest: { $max: "$amountMinor" } } }, // MAX { $sort: { _id: 1 } } // ORDER BY ])

compare.note: The two say the same thing, and both use an index for the WHERE part. The difference is who decides the order. SQL is declarative: you say what you want, and the planner decides when to filter, group and sort. A pipeline runs its stages in the order you write them, with a few rewrites by the server, so $match belongs first or the index can't help. And a pipeline passes documents, not rows: $group can build arrays ($push) and nested results that SQL would need a second query or JSON functions for.

worked.title: Shape the payment document and its indexes from the access patterns

steps.say: Start from the access patterns of Model the access patterns first, and mark which document answers each one. AP1, the account screen, stays on the account document, with its summary of recent payments kept short by $push and $slice.
steps.code:
AP1  account's recent payments    accounts doc, recentPayments ($push + $slice)
AP2  payment by id                payments._id
AP3  merchant + status, newest     index { merchantId: 1, status: 1, createdAt: -1 }
AP4  idempotency key used once     unique partial index on idempotencyKey
AP6  refunds of a payment          embedded in the payment (bounded)

steps.say: Write one payment the way it will be stored. Amounts are 64-bit whole numbers in minor units (NumberLong), times are dates, and the refunds are inside, with the running total next to them.
steps.code: { _id: "pay-81723", accountId: "A-1001", merchantId: "M-0042", status: "SETTLED", amountMinor: NumberLong(4250), currency: "EUR", createdAt: ISODate("2026-11-07T09:00:00Z"), idempotencyKey: "idem-7f3a", refundedMinor: NumberLong(1250), refunds: [ { refundId: "ref-1", amountMinor: NumberLong(1250), at: ISODate("2026-11-07T10:02:00Z") } ] }

steps.say: Make the shape a rule. The validator fixes the types and caps the array at 20 refunds, which is what made embedding safe. On 9.0, switch an existing collection to constraint once it's clean.
steps.code: db.createCollection("payments", { validator: { $jsonSchema: { bsonType: "object", required: ["accountId", "merchantId", "status", "amountMinor", "createdAt", "refundedMinor", "refunds"], properties: { status: { enum: ["AUTHORIZED", "SETTLED", "FAILED"] }, amountMinor: { bsonType: "long", minimum: 1 }, refundedMinor: { bsonType: "long", minimum: 0 }, refunds: { bsonType: "array", maxItems: 20 } } } } })

steps.say: Create one index for each question that _id doesn't answer, and nothing else. Each one is a sorted list that every write has to keep up to date.
steps.code: db.payments.createIndex({ merchantId: 1, status: 1, createdAt: -1 }) // AP3 db.payments.createIndex({ idempotencyKey: 1 }, // AP4 { unique: true, partialFilterExpression: { idempotencyKey: { $type: "string" } } }) db.payments.createIndex({ "refunds.refundId": 1 }) // support: refund -> payment

steps.say: Check each question with explain() before you ship. You want an IXSCAN, no SORT, and keys examined close to documents returned.
steps.code: cost(db.payments.find({ merchantId: "M-0042", status: "FAILED" }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).limit(5)) // { plan: 'LIMIT > FETCH > IXSCAN', returned: 5, keysExamined: 5, docsExamined: 5 }

lab.title: Store payments as documents: embed, guard, index, aggregate
steps: Make sure Docker is running, then run the tests from the labs folder with the command above. The first run starts one mongo:9.0 container through Testcontainers, a library that starts a database in Docker for a test run. That takes a few seconds, plus the download if you've never run env/mongo.yml. All nine tests fail.

Write addRefund as one updateOne with a guarded filter. The race test fires twenty refunds at once at a payment of 10,000 and expects exactly ten to win.

Write createIndexes, recentByMerchantStatus and dailyTotalsPipeline. The tests run explain() on your query and your pipeline, and check for an IXSCAN, no SORT, and 5 keys and 5 documents for 5 results. Swap status and createdAt in your index and watch the AP3 test fail.

The guard compares two fields of the same document, so it needs Filters.expr: Document("\$lte", listOf(Document("\$add", listOf("\$refundedMinor", refund.amountMinor)), "\$amountMinor")). Return modifiedCount == 1L.

The pipeline is listOf(Aggregates.match(...), Aggregates.group("\$status", Accumulators.sum("count", 1), ...), Aggregates.sort(Sorts.ascending("_id"))). The day runs from day.atStartOfDay(ZoneOffset.UTC) to the next day's start, with the end left out.

drill.title: The guarded refund and the write concerns, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the mongosh updateOne that adds a refund ref-2 of 1,250 to payment pay-81723, only if the payment is SETTLED and the refunds stay within the amount. Then write one line each: what w: 1 and w: "majority" promise when the app hears OK, and what happens to each if the primary is cut off right after.

answer.html: db.payments.updateOne( { _id: "pay-81723", status: "SETTLED", $expr: { $lte: [{ $add: ["$refundedMinor", 1250] }, "$amountMinor"] } }, // the guard { $push: { refunds: { refundId: "ref-2", amountMinor: NumberLong(1250), at: new Date() } }, $inc: { refundedMinor: NumberLong(1250) } }) // one document: atomic // modifiedCount 1: applied. 0: not settled, or it would refund too much. // w: 1 the primary has it. Cut off now: rolled back when it rejoins, client never told. // w: "majority" 2 of 3 members have it. Cut off now: any new primary has it too. It survives. // wtimeout hit error to the client, but the write isn't undone: treat it as unknown.

recap: A MongoDB document is a tree of typed fields stored as BSON, with an _id and a 16 MB limit. A write to one document is atomic, so embed what's read and changed together and stays small, like a payment's refunds, and guard the change in the update's filter.
Validators give a collection a schema. strict checks every write, and 9.0's constraint level also checks every document already there before it switches on.

explain() shows what a query read: IXSCAN keys, FETCHed documents, a COLLSCAN of everything, an in-memory SORT. Covered queries read no documents, array fields make multikey indexes, and a unique index on an optional field must be partial.
An aggregation pipeline passes documents through stages such as $match, $group and $sort. Put $match first, so an index can serve it.

A PostgreSQL jsonb column is the same model inside a table: one guarded UPDATE is atomic, a CHECK constraint plays the validator, and joins and transactions over many rows come with it. MongoDB adds sorted indexes on paths inside the document, and sharding.
The limit: a document is safe on one machine, but in a replica set only a write that a majority has survives a failover. A w: 1 write can be rolled back into a file, with no error to the app.

explain.prompt: A teammate wants to set w: 1 on the payments collection: "we measured writes 3 ms faster, and an OK is an OK". Explain what w: 1 and w: "majority" each promise, and what happens to a w: 1 payment in a failover.
explain.answer: With w: 1, the app hears OK as soon as the primary has the write in its oplog. With w: "majority", it waits until two of our three members have it, which in a healthy set costs a few milliseconds. The difference shows only in a failover. If the primary is cut off, the other two elect a new primary after about 10 seconds. A member votes only for a candidate whose oplog is at least as recent as its own, so every write a majority acknowledged is on the new primary. A w: 1 write that hadn't reached a secondary isn't. When the old primary rejoins, it finds the last oplog entry it shares with the new primary and rolls back everything after it into a BSON file in its rollback folder. The payment we confirmed is gone from the collection, and no one gets an error. Three milliseconds isn't worth that for payments. Keep the default w: "majority", and treat a write concern timeout as unknown, because that write isn't undone either.

deeper.html:
Reads have a dial too, the read concern. local, the default, can return writes that are later rolled back. majority returns only what a majority holds, and linearizable reads from the primary and sees every majority write that finished before the read began. MongoDB's causally consistent sessions promise that you read your own writes and never see time go backwards across members. The page on defaults is precise about when: only if the session's reads use majority read concern and its writes use majority write concern. The Replication track's lesson on follower lag names these promises and shows where each one breaks.

Jepsen, a project that tests databases by breaking their networks, published its analysis of MongoDB 4.2.6 in 2020. Transactions ignored the database's and the collection's settings and fell back to local reads and w: 1 writes, unless the transaction set its own. Under network cuts, Jepsen lost acknowledged writes. Other anomalies showed up even at the strongest settings, which MongoDB traced to a retry bug, with a fix planned for 4.2.8. The advice still stands for every version: set read and write concern on each transaction yourself, snapshot and majority.

In 2012, Daniel Abadi's PACELC paper classed MongoDB as PA/EC (the letters say what a system gives up during a network cut, and in normal running), partly because its copies didn't wait for each other and because of its rollback folder. The default became w: "majority" in 5.0, so the class describes a setting of its time, not the product. The first lesson of the Consistency and consensus track uses PACELC properly.

The oplog is a capped collection: when it's full, the oldest entries go. A secondary that falls further behind than the oldest entry can't catch up by replaying, and needs a full copy from scratch. Size the oplog for your longest expected outage, maintenance included.

An arbiter is a member that votes but holds no data. With two data members and one arbiter, a majority of data members is impossible while one is down, so MongoDB's default write concern drops to w: 1 for such sets. That's one more reason to run three members that hold data.

The MongoDB docs say an election should usually finish within 12 seconds, and that a primary that can see only a minority of members steps down by itself.
